english:
It has been very clearly set forth that man is naturally a sociable being[^2], and that his nature (requires) that he live in society[^3]; he is not like the other animals, for whom meeting in society is not a necessity. By reason of the manifold composition of this (human) species, — for, as you know, it is that which is most composite[^4], — there is, between its individuals, a difference so varied that one finds almost no two individuals in harmony under any moral respect whatever, no more than one could find two figures perfectly similar[^1]. That which is the cause of it is the difference of complexion, which produces a difference in the (respective) matters and also in the accidents which accompany the form; for every physical form has certain particular accidents which accompany it, besides the accidents which accompany the matter. So great a variation from individual to individual is not encountered in any species of animals; on the contrary, the difference between the individuals of each species is little perceived[^2], except in man. Indeed, one may find two individuals who differ so much in every moral quality, that one would say they belong to two (different) species, so that you will find (e.g.) such an individual who has cruelty to the point[^3] of slaughtering his young son in the violence of anger, while another is moved (at the idea) of killing a gnat or a reptile, having a soul too tender for that; and it is the same in most of the accidents[^4].

[^2]: See the *Politics* of Aristotle, Book I, ch. 1: ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτιϰὸν ζῶον. Cf. the IIIrd part of this work, ch. XXVII.
[^3]: Literally: *that he be reunited* (with his fellows).
[^4]: We remark in the whole of sublunary beings a progression from the less perfect to the more perfect. Besides the four elements, of which all beings are composed, plants have the vegetative soul, to which, in animals, is joined the vital soul; man alone possesses also the rational soul and is thus found to be the most composite and the most perfect of all sublunary beings.
[^1]: Literally: *that you find almost no two individuals who are in agreement, in any manner whatever, in one of the species of morals, if it be not as you find their exterior figures in agreement*. Instead of אלא מא, the Leyden MS., No. 18, carries כמא לא, and likewise Ibn-Tibbon: כמו שלא תראה; Al-’Harîzi translates: אלא כשתמצא.
[^2]: Literally: *is close or tends to be close.*
[^3]: Instead of לחיים, *to the limit*, *at the point*, the Leyden MS., No. 18, has the words אלי חד, which have the same sense; the version of Ibn-Tibbon has simply עד, *until;* likewise Ibn-Falaquéra, *Moré ha-Moré*, p. 116.
[^4]: That is to say, in most of the moral qualities of the soul.
tr_notes: The term 'complexion' is used in the sense of the humoral or physical constitution of the individual.
The Latinate 'accidents' is used to render 'accidents' as per the glossary's preference for philosophical precision.

english:
Now, as the human species, by its nature, involves this variation among its individuals[^5], and as social life is necessary to its nature, it is absolutely impossible that society be perfect without its having a guide who can regulate the actions of individuals, by supplying what is defective and moderating what is in excess[^1], and who can prescribe actions and morals that all must continually practice, according to the same rule, so that the natural variation be hidden by the great conventional harmony and that society be in good order.

[^5]: Literally: *as its nature* (that of the human species) *requires that there be this variation among its individuals.*
[^1]: Instead of the first אלמפרט, which must be pronounced المفرط, some MSS. carry אלמקצר.
tr_notes: The term 'morals' here renders 'mœurs', referring to the habitual conduct or character of individuals.

english:
Therefore I say that the law, although it be not *natural*, yet enters, in certain respects, into the category of the natural[^2]; for it was of the divine wisdom, in order to preserve this species whose existence it had willed, to place in its nature (the condition) that its individuals should possess a *faculty of regime.* Sometimes the individual is that very one to whom this regime was inspired, and that is the prophet or the legislator; sometimes he is the one who has the faculty to constrain (men) to practice what those two[^3] have prescribed, to follow it and to bring it into actuality, and such are the sovereign who adopts this law (of the legislator) and the pretended prophet who adopts the law of the (true) prophet, either in its entirety or in part. If (the latter) adopts one part and abandons another part[^4], it is either because that is easier for him, or because, through jealousy, he wishes to make it believed that these things reached him through (divine) revelation and that he did not borrow them from another; for there is such a man who takes pleasure in a certain perfection, finds it excellent and is fond of it, and who wishes that men imagine that he is himself endowed with this perfection, although he well knows that he possesses no perfection. Thus it is that you see many men who boast of the poem of another and attribute it to themselves; and this is also what has been done for certain works of the learned and for many scientific details, (I mean) that a jealous and lazy person, having stumbled (by chance) upon a thing invented by another, claimed to have invented it. This is also what happened for this prophetic perfection; for we find that certain men, claiming to be prophets, said things that had never been revealed by God[^1], as (did), for example, Sidkia, son of Kenaana[^2], and we find others who, arrogating prophecy to themselves, said things that, doubtless, God had said, I mean that they had been revealed, but to others, as (did), for example, Hanania, son of Azzour[^3], — so that they attributed them to themselves and adorned themselves with them.

[^2]: Literally: *has yet an entry into the natural thing.*
[^3]: That is to say, the prophet and the legislator. Ibn-Tibbon has מה שצוה הנביא ההוא, *what that prophet prescribed;* likewise Al-’Harîzi, במה שצוה הנביא, and Ibn-Falaquéra (*l. c.*), מה שאמר אותו הנביא. This translation is justified only by a single one of our MSS., No. 18 of Leyden, which carries: בעמל מא גׄא בה אלנביא.
[^4]: Instead of ותרך, the Leyden MS., No. 18, has ותרבה with a suffix. Ibn-Tibbon has והנּיח, without a suffix. At the beginning of the sentence Ibn-Tibbon has ויהיה, while all the Arabic MSS. have יכון, without the copulative ו; הקצתו in the editions of Ibn-Tibbon is a printing error for הקצת.
[^1]: In the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, the words מאת השם are missing here; the MSS. carry: מה שלא באה נבואה בו מאת השם יום כלל. The translator employed the word יום as an adverb, in the sense of *never*, in imitation of the Arabic adverb يوماً.
[^2]: See I Kings, ch. 22, vv. 11 and 24.
[^3]: See Jeremiah, ch. 28, v. 1 et seq. — This example, at first sight, does not seem well chosen, since Hanania, as well as Sidkia, is presented as a false prophet, and his words are expressly belied by Jeremiah. Ibn-Caspi, in his commentary entitled עמודי כסף, raises this difficulty in these terms: תמה איך יאמר הר״מ זה כי עליו כתוב comme על צדקיה כי סרה דבר ובכלל לא מצאתי הבדל בין צדקיה וחנניה. But, in establishing here a distinction between Sidkia and Hanania, Maimonides has only followed the Talmud, according to which the former would have predicted *things which he had never heard* (מתנבא מה שלא שמע), while the latter would have predicted *what had not been said to him* (מתנבא מה שלא נאמר לו), i.e., that he would have done nothing but reproduce a prophecy of Jeremiah, of which he would have distorted the sense or which he would have misunderstood. According to the Jerusalem Talmud (treatise *Synhedrin* last chapter), Hanania, in predicting that, *within two years*, God would break the yoke of the king of Babylon, would have believed himself to be in agreement with Jeremiah, who predicted *seventy years of captivity* (Jeremiah, 29, 10), which, in the opinion of Hanania, had begun during the reign of Manasseh. According to the Babylonian Talmud (same treatise, fol. 89 *a*), the words of Hanania: *I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon*, would be only the reproduction of the words of Jeremiah (49, 35): *behold, I break the bow of Elam;* since, Hanania said to himself, the Elymeans, who were only the auxiliaries of Babylon, were to receive celestial punishment, a fortiori the Chaldeans themselves.
tr_notes: The term 'actuality' renders 'acte' as per the terminology glossary.
The phrase 'faculty of regime' is used to render 'faculté de régime', implying a capacity for governance or systematic order.

english:
All this is recognized and distinguished very clearly; but I shall set it forth to you, so that nothing obscure may remain for you, and that you may possess a *criterion* by means of which you may make the distinction between the regimes of conventional laws[^1], those of the Divine Law, and those emanating from men who have made borrowings from the words of the prophets, by boasting of them and attributing them to themselves. As for the laws which their authors have expressly declared to be the work of their reflection[^2], you have no need[^3] for that of any argumentation, the confession of the adversary rendering all proof unnecessary. I wish therefore only to make known to you the regimes which are proclaimed prophetic, and which, in part, are really prophetic, I mean divine, in part legislative, and in part plagiarisms[^4].

[^1]: That is to say, the regimes or the governments founded by a simple legislator. — Several editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon carry המונחים לא המושמים; instead of לא, one must read ל״א, abbreviation of לשון אחר, for the words המונחים and המושמים are two different translations of the Arabic word
